content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 25 minutes including prep.
is the Japanese take on fried rice. It is lighter and less oily than the Chinese-style version. The goal is
, the faint smokiness and char you can only get from very high heat. Using
that has spent a night in the fridge is the most important rule in the whole recipe.

Heat the wok until it smokes before adding any oil. This is non-negotiable for proper wok-hei. Work in small batches if your hob is not very powerful. Crowding a cool wok steams the rice rather than frying it. Move quickly once the ingredients are in. Fried rice waits for no one.

items.prepNote: finely sliced, white and green separated

content.text: Break up the cold rice with your hands or a fork before you start. Every grain should be separate. Remove any clumps.
Place a wok over the highest heat your hob can produce. Leave it for 2 to 3 minutes until the wok is very hot and just beginning to smoke.
Add the vegetable oil. It should shimmer immediately. Add the white parts of the spring onions and the garlic. Toss for 30 seconds.

Add the cold rice. Press it against the hot wok surface and leave it for 30 seconds without stirring. This is what creates the char. Then toss and press again. Repeat for 2 to 3 minutes until the rice is hot and a few grains have started to colour.

Push the rice to the sides of the wok. Pour the beaten eggs into the centre. Scramble quickly with a spatula. Once the egg is about 70 per cent set, toss the rice back into the eggs and stir everything together.
Add the soy sauce around the edge of the wok, not in the centre. This lets it hit the hot metal and caramelise before mixing in. Add the sesame oil. Toss vigorously for 30 seconds.
Remove from the heat. Scatter over the green spring onion tops and sesame seeds. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The rice is wet and clumping
items.cause: Freshly cooked rice was used or the wok was not hot enough
items.fix: Always use rice that has been cooked and refrigerated for at least one night. Make sure the wok is properly smoking before the oil goes in.

items.symptom: The egg has turned rubbery and overcooked
items.cause: Egg was scrambled too long before the rice was added
items.fix: Add the rice to the egg while it is still quite runny. The egg will finish cooking as it coats the rice grains.

items.symptom: The fried rice has no wok-hei flavour
items.cause: Hob heat was too low or the quantity too large for one batch
items.fix: Fry in two smaller batches on a domestic hob rather than one large batch. Each batch gets better contact with the heat.

content.text: Yakimeshi arrived in Japan via Chinese fried rice techniques, adapted over decades into a lighter, more restrained style. It is a fixture of Japanese home cooking as a way to use up leftover rice. The simplest version uses only egg, soy and spring onion. More elaborate versions add ham, prawns or mixed vegetables. Unlike Chinese chahan, which sometimes uses day-old rice as well, yakimeshi tends to avoid heavy sauces and uses soy more sparingly, letting the smoky char of the wok do the flavour work.
